consensus.claim: Hybrid retrieval (BM25 lexical + dense vectors, RRF/weighted fusion, wide top-k, cross-encoder rerank) outperforms either path alone on mixed identifier-heavy + paraphrase queries; pure dense fails silently on exact identifiers and rare terms.
LLM-as-judge carries position, verbosity, and self-preference biases; trustworthy use requires swap/length controls, task-specific rubrics, and reported human agreement — never bare judge scores.

Small contrastively fine-tuned classifiers (SetFit/IntentBERT-style) reach near-full-data intent accuracy with 8-20 examples per class at a fraction of LLM cost/latency; LLMs add accuracy headroom plus OOS handling at high cost.
Selective prediction / escalation must be scored with risk-coverage curves and AURC against a MaxProb baseline with a held-out calibration split; uncalibrated fixed thresholds prove nothing.

Golden-set annotation requires written guidelines, edge-case adjudication (not averaging), and chance-corrected agreement (Cohen kappa / Fleiss / Krippendorff alpha) before any headline metric is quoted.
Customer-support chatbots need PII redaction, prompt-injection guardrails, and explicit escalation paths; support prompts otherwise leak data and follow injected instructions.

Twitter-support rows are not independent utterances: conversation threading (inbound/outbound, multi-turn, response linkage) must be reconstructed before sampling, splitting, or retrieval; row-level splits leak.

For single-shot classify-retrieve-generate-escalate workloads, a plain pipeline (direct LLM calls + stores) beats agent frameworks on debuggability, latency, and maintenance; frameworks must prove a measured win.

method: independence-weighted: $HPR sources independence scored 70 notes in 0 duplicate clusters; every source counts mass 1.0; consensus threshold mass >= 3.0
